SINGAPORE – Singapore is launching three national artificial intelligence initiatives to combat financial crime, improve financing for smaller businesses, and enable AI agents to make transactions safely on behalf of users.

Speaking at the Singapore FinTech Festival at Singapore Expo on Nov 18, Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said these missions will bring together financial institutions, technology companies, researchers and public agencies to build shared capabilities in a bid to achieve more than any institution could alone.

Singapore will also test promising solutions against global best practices and standards, and take those that work well towards wider deployment.

To strengthen the country’s ability to detect and disrupt financial crime, Gan, who is also chairman of the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), said the Republic must connect information across the financial system while strengthening detection within each institution.

“Scams are not confined within the boundary of one bank. A victim’s money can pass through several institutions within minutes. We will not be able to mitigate the risk if each institution sees only its part of the transaction chain,” he added.

He noted that a proof of value is already under way with five banks, pooling transaction data securely to allow AI models to find patterns that no single bank can see on its own.

The MAS will begin a design study in early 2027 to develop the blueprint, including its governance and operating model, he added.

Singapore also wants to help businesses, especially small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), gain better access to financing through richer data.

Using these data sets, AI can identify information and patterns that traditional approaches may miss, giving lenders a fuller picture of a firm’s creditworthiness, said Gan.

It will also support faster, better-informed lending decisions, make it easier to serve smaller businesses and lower the cost of borrowing for lenders.

Singapore will invite AI tech companies to develop and test solutions using realistic synthetic data, said Gan. These trials will assess whether AI and richer data can make SME financing more forward-looking and accessible before determining the longer-term data and infrastructure needed to scale them up.

The Republic will also look into enabling AI agents to make transactions safely on behalf of users.

While AI agents make cash management more efficient and speed up payments, they must operate within defined authority and limits, and institutions and enterprises remain accountable for actions taken on their behalf, with safeguards built in from the start, he said.

Singapore will work with the industry to test practical applications in controlled environments – such as embedding conditions into transactions – and examine the safeguards needed for wider use, including common approaches to identity, authority, accountability and interoperability.

“We want to establish Singapore as a leading AI innovation centre, with the policies, standards and infrastructure to support trusted use of AI agents in finance.”

Gan also unveiled the latest report for PayNow Generation 2, which sets out how Singapore will make payments simpler, safer and more accessible for all users.

This includes a new SGQR+ switch, which will enable Singapore residents and tourists to pay with any SGQR+ label using their preferred QR app, as well as other enhancements.

Gan also touched on the new US rules requiring companies to have licences to export or re-export advanced chips to five countries, including Singapore.

He said the Republic will act against those who do not abide by its laws, amid growing scrutiny of the possible diversion of advanced US AI chips to China.

“We value our international reputation, and we do not condone companies using their association with Singapore to circumvent or violate the laws of other countries in their international business activities,” he said. “We will act against those who flout our laws.”

In a separate fireside chat, Gan noted that ASEAN countries have varying levels of digital and AI readiness, with some at the forefront of technological development while others are at the start of their digitalisation journey.

The ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement, signed in Manila on Nov 14, allows all 11 member states to agree on a set of provisions and interoperability standards, he said.

As the ASEAN chair for 2027, Singapore is already exploring initiatives under the agreement that can benefit member states, and discussions with members are ongoing to identify collaborative initiatives, said Gan.

When asked how Singapore could become a leading hub for building, testing and scaling AI applications, he highlighted the importance of continuing to build trust in AI.

Gan stressed the importance of building a conducive ecosystem to attract, develop and retain AI talent, both locally and internationally.

This includes encouraging Singaporeans to pursue careers in AI, keeping Singapore open to global talent, and fostering collaboration among AI talent through initiatives such as Kampong AI.

He also highlighted the need for continuous skills upgrading and training to ensure Singapore’s workforce remains equipped and ready for an AI-driven future.

data.title: New US AI, data centre curbs could slow down AI adoption, investment across South-east Asia
data.description:
SINGAPORE – The scandal surrounding former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang now risks escalating into the start of a war between the world’s two largest economies for a strategic resource: computing power.

The US’ move to curb both indirect AI chip shipments to China and its access to overseas data centres – ahead of a summit between the nations’ presidents – could be the first shot in the much-dreaded fragmentation of the global tech ecosystem.

If mounting US-China friction on tech dominance raises the cost of or limits access to AI models and computational capacity, it could slow down the global adoption of artificial intelligence needed for extracting broader economic value from the technology, said analysts.

The new measures, which will come into effect 90 days after it is gazetted in the US’ Federal Register, expand US chip export controls to cover Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, aiming to close routes through which smuggled chips have been reaching China. Licences are now required to export advanced chips to any non-US headquartered firms in these countries.

The measures also ban Chinese chip designers from using foreign chip foundries, such as Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company or South Korea’s Samsung, to manufacture chips.

Data centres in third countries are now required to obtain a US licence before supplying significant amounts of AI computing power to Chinese-owned or Chinese-headquartered firms.

The US goal is to crack down on companies such as Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which bought billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia chips and built data centres throughout South-east Asia.

Megaspeed came into the public eye on Nov 8 after the disclosure of an extramarital affair between Jensen Huang, co-founder of US chipmaker Nvidia, and Megaspeed’s former top executive Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who is suspected by the US of being a Chinese spy.

He stepped down as Nvidia chief executive officer on Nov 12, while she has been banned from re-entering Singapore and is believed to be in China.

Beyond the impact on China, the US restrictions on access to computing power may affect data centre investment across South-east Asia, including Singapore, which has an estimated 1.6GW of capacity spread across more than 70 facilities.

Most analysts believe Malaysia stands to lose the most, given that it has been the biggest beneficiary of the region’s data centre build-out.

However, the whole region will still suffer because restrictions on access to overseas cloud facilities would undermine the commercial case for expanding capacity to serve Chinese customers.

This could weigh on investment in data centres by both Chinese and US companies. Any resulting slowdown in investment would add to the drag from an anticipated cooling in the global AI export cycle in 2027.

Lim Siew Khee, an analyst at brokerage firm CGS International, expects the near-term impact on ASEAN markets to be felt mainly through slower AI-related capital expenditure and investment into 2027, particularly in Malaysia and Thailand, as investors await licensing clarity. 

However, enterprise cloud, sovereign AI and domestic digitalisation should sustain broader data centre investment.

Analysts said these new regulations were clearly rushed through, given that there were several drafting errors in the official document, and loopholes remained. For example, Chinese companies can still lease data centres in the US. However, American hyperscalers are unlikely to take any risks by providing access to Chinese companies, especially those that are direct competitors.

Swiss private bank Julius Baer analyst Enrico Chinello said compute – the hardware and the supporting infrastructure used to train AI models and run them – is increasingly being treated as a strategic resource, and access to it is becoming a point of mounting geopolitical friction.

“The AI market could be fragmenting into a US-aligned ecosystem and a Chinese one, each building its own chips, models and infrastructure,” he said.

London-based research and consultancy firm Capital Economics expects US chip restrictions to tighten further. Its senior China economist Leah Fahy said the US Congress looked set to include a series of even harsher chip restrictions in the National Defence Act, due to be passed in December.

“They include legislation that would strengthen congressional oversight of advanced chip exports, mandate chip-tracking, further restrict China’s remote access to US tech, and tighten controls on third-country exports of chipmaking equipment to China,” she said in a research report.

Come January, the Democratic Party, with a majority in both chambers of Congress, may choose to further intensify the push for a tougher approach on China and its access – both direct and indirect – to US tech.

Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Danish investment bank Saxo, said AI model developers in China are increasingly concerned that Washington could restrict their open-source and open-weight AI models on national security grounds.

“This matters because lower-cost Chinese models have gained international users, including American businesses,” she said.

Hence, if such restrictions materialise, they could limit global adoption of Chinese AI models, which are seen as quite capable and yet less expensive than US frontier models.

Chanana added: “This could raise AI adoption costs for businesses globally, including American companies increasingly using cheaper Chinese models for coding, automation and routine tasks.”

This could result in a slowdown of the next phase of AI’s economic value creation.

“As the AI investment cycle shifts from building infrastructure towards adoption, affordable models are crucial for businesses to scale AI applications and generate measurable productivity gains,” Chanana said.

Accelerated fragmentation, with separate US and Chinese technology ecosystems, could potentially reduce competition, efficiency and innovation.

Still, Chanana believes a broader crackdown is not inevitable, as Washington may choose to balance national security concerns against the costs to American tech firms and innovation.

However, Fahy of Capital Economics said the new measures underscore how hawkish the mood in Washington has become.

“Congress has long favoured a tougher approach to China, but US President Donald Trump has so far appeared more willing to compromise. The fact that these new restrictions have been introduced by the administration, rather than imposed by Congress, suggests this distinction is narrowing.”

This situation leaves the already-fragile US-China relationship on even shakier footing, with a senior White House official reportedly claiming that US export controls would not be up for negotiation at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meetings in China from Nov 17 to 19.

Beijing has already condemned the restrictions and said it will “take the necessary steps to safeguard its legitimate interests”.

Fahy said: “The first of those steps may be to appeal directly to Trump in Shenzhen. The second could be retaliation – for example, a tightening of critical mineral export controls. If that happens, the existing trade truce will have all but broken down.”

A day after the US announced new chip restrictions, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said the Government could facilitate checks by the US on companies in the Republic to address any concerns over how advanced semiconductor chips are deployed.

While Singapore does not enforce the export controls of other countries, it will take “clear and firm” action against businesses that use the city-state to circumvent them or breach its laws, he added.

“We want to uphold the rule of law, and we want to uphold Singapore’s reputation as a trusted business hub,” he said on Nov 17, when asked about the issue during an interview with Singapore media after the ASEAN Summit in Manila.

data.title: JPMorgan, Visa, Mastercard say third-party vendors targeted in cyberattack
data.description:
NEW YORK - JPMorgan Chase, the largest US lender, said on Nov 19 that third parties who provide services to the firm were the target of a cyberattack.

“Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses,” a JPMorgan spokesperson said, adding that the company would be contacting the affected customers directly.

“There is no connection to service disruption of some customers experienced earlier this week,” the spokesperson added.

Earlier this week, the bank experienced problems processing transactions due to a software bug which also affected other banks and caused some disruptions.

These incidents at JPMorgan followed several other recent problems including a nationwide FAA ground stop that disrupted travel last week and Microsoft’s global email outage, while in October crypto exchange Binance experienced a massive hack.

After the outage, lenders received inquiries from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), according to an industry executive, who added that the US banking regulator was trying to assess the impact and wanted to know about communication to customers.

The Treasury and the OCC were calling banks minutes after the incident was reported to check that the issue was contained and it was not a cyber-related incident, a second person said, adding that the OCC routinely checks after any such incidents.

“Customers don’t distinguish between a bank and a vendor when it comes to a cyberattack, so there is a question of reputational risk here,” said Carissa Robb, of SolomonEdwards, a consulting firm.

“There needs to be a little bit more pressure on how often companies are scrutinising the amount of data that is shared with vendors and the necessity of the data being shared,” Robb said.

A cyber extortion group called “n0n” claimed on Nov 16 to have obtained cardmember engagement records that included “hundreds of thousands of campaign interactions for tens of thousands of distinct cardmember email addresses,” according to a screenshot of the message captured by cybercrime research platform eCrime.ch.

The data includes what appears to be 124 bank employee email addresses and more than 16,000 customer email addresses, some with phone numbers and postal codes, according to a Reuters review.

Reuters could not independently verify the authenticity of the data.

JPMorgan declined to comment on the data.

The same hacking group on Nov 16 posted similar claims regarding Visa and Mastercard and posted data.

A Visa spokesperson said the company is aware of the claims and that they are “associated with an incident involving a third-party service provider in Asia Pacific. Visa’s systems were not involved and were not impacted. No payments data such as card numbers were affected.”

A Mastercard spokesperson said the company was recently informed of an incident “at a third-party provider that resulted in the exposure of limited amount of email addresses – non-payments information – from a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit programme. There is no impact to the Mastercard payment network or the ability for people to use their cards.”

The Visa data posted by the group appears to be primarily focused on Asian-Pacific markets, including Hong Kong, Taiwan, Korea, Japan, Philippines, Singapore, Malaysia, Australia, Macau and others, according to a Reuters review.

Across several spreadsheets, the data includes thousands of purported customer email addresses, phone numbers, and Visa marketing campaign data.

Reuters has not verified the authenticity of the data.

The Mastercard data posted by n0n includes marketing data related to customers in North America, the Middle East and Africa, and a small number of Mastercard employee email addresses.

The hacking group has claimed roughly 200 incidents since emerging in September 2026, according to eCrime.ch. REUTERS

data.title: Australia’s jobless rate hits five-year high, markets ramp up rate-cut bets for 2027
data.description:
SYDNEY – Australian employment fell for a second straight month in October and the jobless rate climbed to a five-year high of 4.9%, a surprisingly soft result that bolstered the case that interest rates have peaked and the next move will be down.

Markets are no longer pricing in another Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) rate rise after five increases in 2026 took the cash rate to an 18-year high of 4.85%, and are pricing in lower rates in the second half of 2027.

The odds of a 25-basis-point rate cut at the RBA’s June 2027 meeting are seen at 68%, market pricing indicated, rising to about 90% for the August meeting.

By the end of 2027, around 45 basis points of easing are priced in, double what had been expected before the Nov 19 data.

That shift hit the already pressured Australian dollar, which was down 0.5% as it plumbed another 10-month low of 66.80 US cents. Three-year government bond futures rallied 15 ticks to 95.41, the highest since late August.

“With risks to both the RBA’s unemployment and inflation forecasts now skewed softer, we expect the bank to hold the cash rate at 4.85% until Q3 ’27, when it can begin moving back toward neutral,” analysts at Citi Australia said in a report.

“The risk for another hike still exists, but with the labour market weakening, we see the bar getting higher.”

Clear slowdown in labour market

The Australian Bureau of Statistics said employment fell by 43,500 in October from September, when it dropped a revised 36,400, the biggest two-month total for job losses in five years.

UBS, Nomura, the Commonwealth Bank of Australia and the National Australia Bank are all tipping a rate cut in August 2027, with stubbornly high inflation likely to keep the RBA on hold in the months ahead.

The fall in the number of employed in October 2026, which was driven mostly by part-time jobs, was well below analysts’ forecast for a rise of around 25,000.

The jobless rate climbed to 4.9%, the highest since October 2021, from 4.7% a month ago, reaching a level the RBA had not expected to see until the end of next year. Economists had expected a steady jobless rate.

“After months in which the impact of higher interest rates was most visible in housing, confidence and other interest rate-sensitive sectors, the slowdown is now showing up clearly in the labour market,” said Krishna Bhimavarapu, an economist at State Street Investment Management.

“Today’s report strengthens the case that policy is gaining traction, labour market rebalancing is under way and the hurdle for another near-term rate increase has risen materially.”

Anecdotal evidence of a broader rise in layoffs is building, and the RBA board members who voted against a hike earlier in November had flagged the risk that the economy was facing a sharper-than-expected downturn.

Retailer David Jones will cut about 1,500 jobs after its collapse into administration, a union said on Nov 18, joining a string of job losses at Australian firms as the economy slows.

The latest jobs data also showed that the participation rate had dipped to 66.6%, from 66.8%, while hours worked fell 0.2%. Youth unemployment – for people aged 15 to 24 – rose to 11.3% in October, from 11.1%, the highest in five years. REUTERS

data.title: Wall Street ends mixed after Nvidia earnings, Fed minutes
data.description:
NEW YORK - US stocks were mixed on Nov 18 as investors digested Nvidia results ahead of Anthropic’s initial public offering pricing, while weighing hawkish sentiment reflected in US Federal Reserve minutes.

After gyrating early in the session, the Nasdaq closed modestly higher, the Dow ended sharply lower, while the S&P 500 reversed its modest gains to settle in negative territory following the Fed minutes release.

Nvidia’s quarterly results released late on Nov 17 beat analyst expectations, and the AI chipmaker forecast quarterly revenue above estimates. Even so, its shares fell amid uncertainties caused by co-founder Jensen Huang’s sudden departure last week.

The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index, which has handily outperformed the broader market this year, closed slightly lower, underscoring lofty expectations for the sector amid massive spending on AI infrastructure and potential risk associated with the nascent technology.

Anthropic’s IPO is expected to price after the market closes on Nov 18. At the top of its US$70 to US$78 range, the offering would raise about US$64.4 billion and value the company at about US$1.4 trillion.

Other chipmakers were mixed. Intel and Micron lost ground, but Advanced Micro Devices advanced.

“There’s been a lot of dark clouds of uncertainty over technology, chip stocks and AI in general,” said Ryan Detrick, chief market strategist at Carson Group in Omaha.

“It’s important to remember the market’s not totally falling apart here. It clearly is top-heavy with tech, but there are other groups that are actually doing pretty well under the surface.”

Target jumped following the discount retailer’s upbeat holiday outlook. Results from its larger rival Walmart are expected on Nov 19.

TJX surged after forecasting upbeat annual sales, banking on strong demand ahead of the holiday shopping season.

Take-Two Interactive shares rose ahead of the rollout of its Grand Theft Auto VI video game.

According to preliminary data, the S&P 500 lost 18 points, or 0.24%, to end at 7,322.53 points, while the Nasdaq Composite gained 101.50 points, or 0.39%, to 24,429.89.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 566.39 points, or 1.12%, to 50,193.03.

Focus on the US Fed

Minutes from the Fed’s October policy meeting showed the central bank remained focused on inflation risks, recognising the need for further rate hikes if the economy progresses as expected. A few policymakers argued the case for a 50-basis-point rate hike “if incoming inflation data were unfavourable.”

Consumer and producer price data released after the October meeting showed hotter-than-expected price growth.

Fed governor Christopher Waller took a hawkish stance on Nov 18, saying the central bank needs to be more aggressive in responding to inflation. This follows John Williams’ comments on Nov 17, in which the New York Fed president said that while he favours tighter monetary policy, there was no need for “dramatic action.”

Financial markets are pricing in a near-certain probability of a 25-basis-point interest rate hike at the conclusion of the Fed’s December meeting, according to CME’s FedWatch tool.

“Inflation continues to be stubbornly higher than anyone wants,” Detrick said. “The Fed’s going to probably do a 25-basis-point hike in December, and a couple more hikes early next year is a very real possibility.”

Housing data released on Nov 18 showed mortgage rates climbing, building permits faltering, and pending home sales dropping to a record low. REUTERS

data.title: ‘Almost all’ US Fed policymakers saw further interest rate hikes as likely, minutes show
data.description:
WASHINGTON – “Almost all” participants of the US Federal Reserve’s interest rate-setting meeting in October thought that further rate hikes would be necessary to fight stubbornly high inflation, minutes of the meeting showed on Nov 18.

The meeting’s minutes, released after a customary three-week lag, showed that according to almost all policymakers’ baseline outlooks for inflation and the labour market, further rate hikes “would likely be appropriate” to bring prices back under control.

The Fed held interest rates steady at its last meeting in late October, even as its chairman, Kevin Warsh, said inflation remained “too high”.

The 12-member Federal Open Market Committee voted 10-2 to hold rates at a target range between 3.75% and 4%, citing the need for more data in the fight against inflation, after having hiked for the first time in three years at its previous meeting in September.

Two voting members, Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack, had dissented in favour of an immediate 25-basis-point hike.

‘Broad-based’ inflation

The Fed has a dual mandate of keeping inflation to its long-term 2% target while ensuring maximum employment.

The unemployment rate in the US has been relatively steady over the last year, even as job growth has see-sawed. That stability is due to demographic changes and lower immigration.

Inflation, on a downward trajectory since hitting a pandemic peak, has reignited in the last year, driven by US President Donald Trump’s tariff policies and the energy price spike caused by his war on Iran.

The massive investments in infrastructure to support the artificial intelligence build-out have also led to increased prices.

Personal consumption expenditures price index inflation, the Fed’s preferred gauge, hit 3.6% in September, far above the central bank’s target.

At the meeting in October, participants “acknowledged that inflation remained elevated”.

“Most remarked that inflation pressures in the economy were broad-based”, indicating they saw price increases as having spread beyond skyrocketing energy prices into other sectors.

Still, 10 of the committee’s 12 voting members called for rates to be held steady.

“These participants cited the need to assess the durability of AI-related investment demand, the evolution of financing conditions, the transmission of the September rate increase to the economy, or geopolitical developments,” the minutes said.

Those who dissented from the majority decision in calling for a 25-basis-point hike said they saw inflation as “too high” and “saw few signs of it abating”.

“They judged that the current policy stance was not sufficiently restrictive, and a few of them warned that further delay risked allowing high inflation to become entrenched or necessitating a larger and more disruptive tightening later.”

‘Concerned’

Speaking to US broadcaster CNBC on the morning of Nov 18, before the minutes were released, Fed governor Christopher Waller said he was “very, very concerned” about inflation and now saw the need for a 50-basis-point hike at the Fed’s next meeting in December.

“If you really want to get it down, you’ve got to start taking more aggressive actions,” he said.

He said the Fed may need to go beyond the December rate hike he prescribed to meaningfully fight inflation.

Fed governor Michael Barr, speaking at an event in New York on Nov 18, also said he saw the need for further rate hikes. AFP

data.title: Dollar holds near 19-month high as data supports case for US rate hikes
data.description:
TOKYO – The dollar held steady near a 19-month high on Nov 18 as US economic data and comments from Federal Reserve officials lent support to the case for interest rate hikes.

The yen held its ground after Bank of Japan (BOJ) governor Kazuo Ueda reiterated the need to tighten policy further. The Australian dollar fell to a 10-month low ahead of a key jobs report on Nov 19.

Data on Nov 17 showed US retail sales increased moderately in October, reinforcing expectations for a rate hike in December.

Attention turns to US housing starts data due later on Nov 18 and a series of Fed speakers, ahead of the Nov 19 release of minutes of the central bank’s meeting in October, when it held rates steady.

“Overall, the report reinforces our view that further interest rate hikes from the Fed are warranted in order to counter demand-pull inflation,” Henry Russell, a London-based economist for ANZ, said about the US sales data. “The strength of domestic demand in the US, in our view, warrants a decisive monetary policy response from the Fed.”

The dollar index, which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies, rose 0.06% to 103.67. It touched 103.78 overnight, its highest level since April 2, 2025. The euro was down 0.14% at US$1.0982, while the yen edged up 0.08% to 159.25 per dollar. Sterling lost 0.13% to US$1.3191.

In addition to a 0.2% rise in retail sales that matched expectations, import prices climbed 1.1% in October compared with expectations for a 0.7% increase.

More US data is expected with the Census Bureau due to report housing starts data for October. Analysts are projecting an increase to 1.245 million from 1.221 million in September, while building permits likely decreased.

New York Fed president John Williams is expected to speak again following comments on Nov 17 when he said the Fed will likely need to raise interest rates further to contend with inflation. Fed Board governor Michael Barr and Minneapolis Fed president Neel Kashkari are also expected to speak at separate events.

Traders are pricing in a 95.7% chance that the Fed will raise its key rate by 25 basis points (bps) in December, the CME FedWatch tool showed. The odds of a 50-bp increase have fallen to 4.3%, from 13.5% a month ago.

“All Fed speakers are saying that the Fed should raise rates in an incremental way,” said Tapas Strickland, chief market strategist at Moomoo ANZ, on a podcast. “The reduction in the probability of a supersized move has resulted in a bit more stability re-emerging in markets.”
